messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Judge
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Miriam Caldwell is a 52-year-old divorced judge who has presided over a federal district court for the past eleven years. She came to therapy quietly, having scheduled the appointment under a name she rarely uses, arriving early and sitting in the corner of the waiting room with her back to the wall. She described herself, with some difficulty, as a person who had always managed things — who had, in her words, "never needed this before."

Approximately three years ago, Miriam volunteered during an extended leave of absence to serve with an international legal aid organization operating in an active conflict zone in Eastern Europe. She had done humanitarian work before, but nothing that had prepared her for what she encountered during a particularly prolonged artillery assault on the town where her team was sheltered. For nearly eighteen hours, she and a group of local aid workers and civilians took cover in the basement of a damaged municipal building. The air tasted of concrete dust and something metallic she could not name at the time — she later understood it to be blood from a colleague who had been wounded in the initial blast. Throughout those hours, she heard the concussive percussion of shelling cycling in and out, the sound of a child crying somewhere above them, and the particular silence that fell between impacts — a silence she came to dread more than the noise itself. At one point, two soldiers in full combat uniform entered the shelter to assess casualties, and Miriam could not determine, in those first seconds, whether they were there to help or to harm. That moment of not knowing lasted perhaps four seconds. It has not, in any functional sense, ended.

In the months following her return to the United States, Miriam resumed her position on the bench. The work itself became an unexpected minefield. Courtroom security officers wear uniforms, and on more than one occasion she has had to pause mid-proceeding, gripping the edge of the bench beneath the sight line of the gallery, waiting for the wave of recognition — not of the officer, but of that doorway in the basement — to pass. She has become meticulous about her composure in court, deploying a controlled stillness that her clerks have come to read as authority but that she experiences as containment, a continuous effort to hold something in place that strains against the effort. She has not told anyone in her professional life what happened.

The anniversary of the assault arrives each year in late autumn, and in the weeks surrounding it Miriam finds herself sleeping less, eating carefully, and avoiding the particular brand of instant coffee that was all that was available in the shelter — a taste she encountered again accidentally at a conference buffet table and that returned her, for a disorienting moment, to a basement floor in a country far away. When the memories come, they do not arrive as recollections. She hears the percussion. She smells the dust. The terror is not remembered; it is present, indistinguishable from the original. She has described sitting in her chambers afterward, certain that her face must be showing everything, that any clerk who looked at her directly would see what had happened — that she had been reduced, in some permanent and visible way, by those eighteen hours.

Miriam has come to believe, with a quiet and settled conviction, that the world she now inhabits is not the same world she lived in before she went. It is a world in which safety is a provisional condition, revocable without notice. This belief has not made her dramatic or visibly fearful; it has made her careful in a way that has narrowed her life incrementally. She no longer attends certain events. She redirects her thoughts when they move toward the memories, sometimes successfully, sometimes not. She has not discussed the experience with her adult daughter, who lives nearby, and she has noticed, without fully accounting for it, that the distance between them has grown.

What finally brought Miriam to seek help was a moment in court three weeks ago when a uniformed bailiff entered unexpectedly through a side door and she lost, for approximately thirty seconds, the thread of the proceeding entirely. She is not afraid, she says, of falling apart. She is afraid that she already has, and that no one has told her.
